anchors.fact: By the early 1960s some were already making the Margarita in a blender (Oxford, FROZEN DAIQUIRI pdf 854).
anchors.meaning: The blender drink that kept coming out different had been around for years before he got to it.
anchors.speaksTo: the settled answer others lived with

anchors.fact: His blenders couldn't make a consistent mix and his bartenders were "in rebellion" (Smithsonian NMAH record 2005.0226.01); customers complained it was "inconsistent and not even cold" (AP via HNN, 10 Oct 2005). In his words: "a lack of consistency, and my bartenders were threatening to quit", and "we kept burning out the blenders as fast as we could buy them" (*VinePair*, 2021).
anchors.meaning: The everyday shortcoming, on record, in his own words.
anchors.speaksTo: irritation first; the complaint on record

anchors.fact: The idea came from a Slurpee machine at a 7-Eleven (NMAH record; AP 2005); he adapted a soft-serve ice cream machine to make Margaritas at his Dallas restaurant (Oxford, MARGARITA pdf 1237; NMAH).
anchors.meaning: The answer to a restaurant's problem was in a convenience store and an ice-cream machine.
anchors.speaksTo: the new angle: borrowed from somewhere unrelated

anchors.fact: As he tells it, the machine was made to spin faster and given a bigger compressor so the drinks came out colder; "through trial and error, we developed" it (*VinePair*, 2021).
anchors.meaning: Built, not argued; and "properly cold" was part of the fix.
anchors.speaksTo: builds structure: the same every time

anchors.fact: "I never intended to invent something." "I was just trying to make my customers happy." (*VinePair*, 2021, his words; always attributed)
anchors.meaning: The fix was for other people's evenings, not for a name.

anchors.fact: The frozen Margarita machine "would soon be a fixture of the age" (Oxford, MARGARITA pdf 1237); many versions came onto the market; the original is in the Smithsonian's collection, his gift (NMAH record).
anchors.meaning: Others use it without thinking who started it.
anchors.speaksTo: others use it now without thinking

anchors.fact: "The complaints bothered him long before any machine did" is ours. Signposted "I like to think".
anchors.meaning: The hidden annoyance, handed to him gently.

anchors.fact: "the Sidecar's most famous variation is the Margarita" (*Codex* p. 156); "Two famous cocktails, the Margarita and the Cosmopolitan" (*Codex* p. 106).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic, made frozen. The fame is the Margarita's, not the frozen one's.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having

anchors.fact: His father "always insisted on using Cointreau" (Martinez, *VinePair* 2021); Cointreau is "an aromatic, clear liqueur bottled at 40 percent ABV" (Oxford, COINTREAU pdf 551).
anchors.meaning: His family's bottle in the glass, named for them.

anchors.fact: Arnold's freezer method, to "replicate a 7-Eleven-style frozen treat": the whole batch frozen with its water, the lime left out and added at the blend; about 14%, sugar no more than 9 g/100 ml; made "the day before" (*LI* pp. 141–142). Coincidence owned in one clause; Arnold never mentions Martinez.
anchors.meaning: Most of the work done once, so every two glasses after take seconds.
anchors.speaksTo: spend the weekend so you never spend ten minutes

anchors.fact: Citrus is among vanilla's best pairings (*Flavor Matrix* pdf 256); Arnold adds "a drop of vanilla extract" to orange in the Dr. J (*LI* p. 271); vanilla pods ripen at different times and are graded (Matrix pdf 256); that a measured extract is steadier than a pod is Tomás's reasoning, not the page's. "From the ice-cream counter" is our reading.
anchors.meaning: A flavour borrowed from another counter, the way he borrowed a machine, and stable enough to be the same every time.
anchors.speaksTo: borrowed from somewhere unrelated; the same every time

cocktail.closingLine: Make it a day ahead. Then the evening is for your guests, not the blender.
cocktail.glassware: a large stemmed goblet (about 350 ml), chilled, no salt rim
method: A day ahead, stir the tequila, Cointreau, syrup, water and vanilla together in a jug.

Pour half into each of two freezer bags or wide lidded containers, about 450 ml each. Each one makes two drinks. Seal them and lay them flat in the freezer for a day. The alcohol and sugar keep the mix from freezing hard: it sets thick and icy.
If it's still liquid after a day, your freezer isn't quite cold enough. Add the lime (75 ml to each bag) three to six hours before you serve, and it will set.

To serve two, put two goblets in the freezer for ten minutes. Squeeze 75 ml of lime juice, unless it's already in the bag from step 3. Break up one bag with your hands through the plastic, tip it into a blender with the lime, and blend just until smooth and thick, a few seconds. Blending longer only warms it.
Pour into the chilled goblets. No salt and no garnish. The second bag makes the next two, and they'll come out the same.
cocktail.name: For Good

recipe.item: Cointreau (recommended), or any clear orange triple sec at 40%
recipe.note: his father always insisted on Cointreau

recipe.item: simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear)

recipe.note: the melt, measured once, so the ice never decides
orange and vanilla, borrowed from the ice-cream counter

recipe.item: fresh lime juice (about 5 limes), added only when you blend
recipe.note: the one fresh thing, every time

cocktail.tagline: You don't mind losing a weekend if nobody loses ten minutes again.

reading.epigraph: One idea behind this glass came from a convenience store.
whoYouAre: Somewhere in your life there's the proof of how you work: a thing that used to jam, drip or stick, until one afternoon you'd had enough of it. You took it apart there and then, and it hasn't jammed since. And you regret none of it.

What you keep quiet is how it starts. It sounds like moaning: the queue that's slow for no reason, the form that asks for the same thing twice, the way something has always been done that has never quite worked. You've tried sighing and getting on with it. It doesn't take. It stays with you until you've found a way round, and the way round usually comes from somewhere nobody thought to look. The sentence you can't bear is "it's always been like that". The one that frightens you is hearing yourself say it, and meaning it. And the things you fix stay fixed. People stop having the problem, forget it was ever there, and get their afternoons back. That's what your restlessness gives them, and it's worth far more than the grumbling it started with.
yours: By the early 1960s, some people were already making the Margarita in a blender. About ten years later, in Dallas, Mariano Martinez was making frozen ones at his own restaurant, and they weren't working. They kept coming out different, and not even cold, his customers complained. His bartenders were threatening to quit. The restaurant was burning out blenders, he said later, as fast as it could buy them.

The answer wasn't in a bar. It was at a 7-Eleven, in the Slurpee machine. He took a soft-serve ice cream machine and bent it to the job: through trial and error, as he tells it, they made it spin faster and gave it a bigger compressor, so the drinks came out colder. Before long, frozen Margarita machines were a fixture, and many versions came onto the market. The original is in the Smithsonian now. He never meant to invent anything, he said; he was just trying to make his customers happy.

The complaints bothered him long before any machine did, I like to think. You'd know that feeling. You hear the grumble everyone hears, and you're the one who can't let it go. Then you find the fix somewhere nobody thought to look: a restaurant's answer, sitting in a convenience store. And once it works, you're happy for it to disappear. I doubt many people ordering a frozen Margarita today think about Dallas, or burned-out blenders. They just get a cold drink. That's how you look after people: they never have to find out there was a problem.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Margarita, one of the most famous cocktails there is, made frozen, with blanco tequila and Cointreau, the orange liqueur Martinez's father always insisted on. It's built the way you'd build it: most of the work happens once. A day ahead, you mix everything but the lime, water and all, and freeze it in two bags. By coincidence, the book I took the method from describes it as making a 7-Eleven-style frozen treat. After that, every two glasses are one bag from the freezer and the juice of two or three limes, then a few seconds in the blender. There's no ice added and nothing to guess at, so it comes out the same, and properly cold, every time. And there's a little vanilla in the batch, just half a teaspoon. Orange and vanilla always makes me think of the ice-cream counter, so I borrowed it from there, the way he borrowed a machine. It's served thick in a big chilled stemmed glass, with no salt.

So trust the annoyance. It isn't moaning, and it isn't ingratitude. It's usually the first sign that you've found something worth fixing. The next time someone tells you it's always been like that, take it as directions: they've just shown you where to start. And when it works and nobody says a word, enjoy the quiet. You made it.
